A1.justification: Despite the changed title and expanded scope, v2 retains the same private fine-tuning study, linear-network analysis, and transfer-learning benchmarks. Both PDFs provide readable text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices.

before.justification: Section 4, Figure 2, and Table 1 report original fine-tuning experiments across four transfer-learning benchmarks and five architectures.

after.justification: Sections 3.2 and 5.3 and Appendices A and E report fine-tuning accuracies, representation-quality measurements, LoRA comparisons, and numerical simulations.

M1.justification: The LP, full fine-tuning, and sequential LP-FT procedures remain, with FT renamed FFT. Section 5.3 adds LP-LoRA, replacing the second full-fine-tuning stage with low-rank adaptation. This is a limited procedural extension; the extensive new approximation framework primarily changes the theoretical analysis.

E1.justification: The original four transfer benchmarks remain. V2 additionally evaluates MNIST classes 0, 3, and 7, tests feature representations on out-of-distribution CIFAR-10 after STL-10 fine-tuning and on the ImageNet pretraining distribution, and introduces synthetic two-layer-network simulations. This substantially expands the evaluated scenarios beyond downstream classification accuracy.

E2.justification: V1 compares LP, LP-FT, and FT. V2 retains these comparisons and adds a separate Mini-DeiT-Ti comparison of LP, LP-LoRA, and LoRA in Table 2. The comparator expansion is limited to this additional fine-tuning family.

E3.justification: The reported settings for the main accuracy comparison change from batch size 64 to 1000 and from three learning rates, or five for transformers, to nine. New representation experiments specify 100 pretraining epochs, 30 private fine-tuning epochs, and top-1 kNN evaluation. The MNIST study introduces controlled LP durations followed by five FFT epochs with different phase-specific noise multipliers.

E4.justification: V2 adds direct tests of early feature distortion and its mitigation through LP, using kNN trajectories and UMAP visualizations across training stages and domains. It also varies MNIST LP warm-up duration and adds layer-sensitivity and high-noise eigenvalue-error simulations in Figures 9–10. These investigate mechanisms and analytical approximations absent from v1's empirical analyses.

E5.justification: V1 reports three random seeds and standard errors. V2 specifies five seeds for representation experiments and 10,000 seeds, with standard error below 0.001, for Figure 9. Standard-error reporting remains; these disclosures do not establish that the retained experiments were rerun with more seeds.

E6.justification: V2 adds feature-distortion findings, LoRA scores, privacy-budget curves, and simulation results, while revising Table 1. For example, reported non-private ResNet-18 FT accuracy changes from 71.45% to 73.69%; the changed settings prevent treating this as a same-setting gain. V1's MoCo utility curves are retained as v2 Figure 6.

T1.justification: V2 adds a Langevin perturbation approximation, two-layer ReLU/exponential-loss analysis, feature-distortion theorems, approximate upper and lower convergence bounds, relaxed assumptions, and clipped-diffusion analyses. Much of v1's linear theory moves to Appendix E, which adds an explicit numerical Jensen-gap conjecture and associated derivation. V1's Appendix A.5 layer-sensitivity proof is no longer supplied.

C1.justification: V1 centers its contributions on linear-network convergence bounds and the LP-FT privacy-budget trade-off. V2 makes representation distortion, its mitigation through head alignment, and a new approximation supporting nonlinear-network convergence analysis central claims in the abstract and introduction. The original budget-allocation claim remains within this broader contribution.

C2.justification: V2 adds a detailed interpretation of initial feature degradation and subsequent recovery through representation alignment. It acknowledges that Figure 2b departs from the predicted budget-allocation trend and offers explicitly tentative explanations involving distribution mismatch, EMA, and augmentation averaging. Limitations now address local assumptions, deeper networks, other losses, LoRA, generative models, and lower bounds without the approximation.

D1.justification: V2 newly specifies clipping thresholds, LoRA rank 8, simulation configurations, and BatchNorm-to-GroupNorm replacement for the retained utility-curve experiment. It adds a future code-release promise, without establishing actual code availability, and drops v1's explicit pretrained-weight repository pointer. These are useful but limited reproducibility changes.

R1.justification: The new Related Work subsection substantially repositions the paper around in-distribution feature distortion, neural collapse, and architecture-sensitive nonlinear analysis. New references include Wang et al. on neural collapse and privacy, perturbation-method sources, and LoRA. Previously cited work by Kumar and Min receives a substantially expanded role; Min's publication update alone is not an added work.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, contribution list, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. The narrative is reorganized around continuous modeling, representation alignment, convergence, and budget allocation, with experiments integrated into the relevant sections. Much of the original setup, linear analysis, and experimental documentation moves into reorganized appendices.

P2.justification: V2 adds representation diagrams, UMAP panels, feature-quality trajectories, privacy-utility plots, simulation plots, and a LoRA table. Table 1 changes from model/noise rows with parameter counts to architecture-grouped epsilon columns with highlighted entries. The original network schematic is resized and relocated, while v1 Figure 2 is retained as Figure 6.

improvement.justification: V2's direct feature-quality measurements, LoRA comparisons, and more explicit limitations substantially enrich v1's evidence. However, a central new theoretical claim remains internally unresolved: Theorem 5.1 gives privacy-budget scaling proportional to sigma^4, while Appendix D.3, Equation 95 gives LP time proportional to sigma^2 and Theorem 4.1 gives privacy cost scaling as T/sigma^2. The supplied derivation does not reconcile these expressions. The empirical benefits and unresolved reliability of the new quantitative theory prevent a confident overall quality judgment.
